highlights.text: one root whose core notion is **the left-hand side**
الْمَشْأَمَة (al-mashʾama) is the left side
one root whose core idea is seeking and aiming at something
One's concern or pursuit.
not miserliness from you, nor is generosity part of your شَأْن"
highlights.note: unattributed verse, for شَأْن as one's aim

highlights.text: this root has two distinct original meanings: (1) separation/division, and (2) gathering/union
From this comes shaʿb = a "people" — literally a branch that has split off from the Arab and non-Arab tribes
He cites Qur'an 49:13, "We made you into peoples (shuʿūb) and tribes (qabāʾil)."
Roads that diverge, or a tree's branches that split off
A gazelle whose two horns splay far apart is ashʿab — with a terse citation from Abū Duʾād
A hadith is cited using the same root: "What is this ruling that has scattered (shaʿʿabat) the people?"
highlights.note: a hadith, cited for the scattering sense

highlights.text: spreading and dispersing outward from a single thing
ishtaʿalat al-nār means "the fire blazed/flared up."
ishtaʿala al-shayb describes gray hair "spreading" through the head
highlights.note: the sense behind Q 19:4, the entry's own citation

highlights.text: a line of the poet Dhū al-Rumma describing women who deliberately let prayer times pass
highlights.note: Dhū al-Rumma, Umayyad; the entry's only poet

highlights.text: two distinct roots: one meaning firmness/growth, the other meaning knowledge and marking
شَعَرْتُ بِالشَّيْء — I perceived/became aware of a thing
شَاعِر (poet) — so called because he perceives (yafṭin) what others miss.
the sites of the rites, called this because they are the landmarks (maʿālim) of the Ḥajj.
ʿAntara's line "Have the poets left any patch to re-mend?" — i.e. poets have overlooked nothing.
withholding (al-manʿ) as the root meaning of sh-ḥ-ḥ
**al-shuḥḥ**: avarice combined with greed
"whoever is guarded against the shuḥḥ of his own self, those are the ones who thrive."
a line by Ibn Harma about leaving the bounty of the most generous
highlights.note: Ibn Harma, Umayyad; the entry's only poet

highlights.text: this root denotes a category of flesh — namely fatty tissue.
الشَّحْم (ash-shaḥm) — "fat," a well-known, ordinary word needing no further gloss.
two unrelated roots, one meaning "filling," the other "distancing/driving off."
شَحَنْتُ السَّفِينَةَ — "I loaded the ship," i.e. filled it.
derives the root sh-ṭ-ʾ (شطأ) from two unrelated senses.
Shaṭʾ (شَطْء) — a plant's "shoot"
Shāṭiʾ (شَاطِئ) — the "bank" or "side"
two sound root meanings (aṣlān ṣaḥīḥān): distance (al-buʿd) and inclining (al-mayl).
committing shaṭaṭ, which is exceeding the measure
Shaṭṭa and ashaṭṭa denote injustice (jawr) and leaning in judgement
In the report of Tamīm al-Dārī, "surely you are unjust to me, so that I carry your strength on my weakness", the word is explained as "unjust in judging against me".
highlights.note: a report of the Companion Tamīm al-Dārī

highlights.text: a single sound root whose core meaning is remoteness / distance (al-buʿd).
so named for its "remoteness from the truth" and its rebellion (tamarrud)
any insolent rebel, whether jinn, human, or beast, is called a shayṭān
highlights.note: شَيْطَٰن: the ordinary sense of the word

highlights.text: a line of Umayya using the form شَاطِن (shāṭin, pattern fāʿil)
one meaning the half of a thing, the other meaning distance and facing/being opposite.
شَطْر in the sense of the aim and direction of a thing
He cites Q 2:144 on the qibla — "wherever you are, turn your faces شَطْرَهُ"
Two poetic witnesses support this: "set straight the breasts of the pale camels shaṭra (toward) Banū Tamīm,"
highlights.note: unattributed verse, for the directional sense

highlights.text: core meaning is that one thing resembles or matches another
The forms shibh, shabah, and shabīh all mean "a like / the like of something."
a single root meaning strength in a thing
"and truly in his love of wealth he is shadīd,"
highlights.note: شَدِيد, 56 times; the entry cites Q 100:8

highlights.text: a verse of Ṭarafa: "I see death choosing the noble and selecting the choicest part of the wealth of the tight-fisted miser (al-mutashaddid)."
a single sound root whose core idea is pairing or joining one thing to another.
الشَّفْع (al-shafʿ) means "even," the opposite of الوتر (al-watr, "odd")
شَفَعَ لفلان is to come as someone's "second," seeking his request and helping him.
reports the exegetes' reading that al-watr is God and al-shafʿ is creation.
الشُّفْعَة (al-shufʿa), a claimant's right of pre-emption over a house
al-shafah — the lip
thinness or fineness in something
أَشْفَقْتُ مِنَ الْأَمْرِ means to be wary and cautious of a matter
al-shafaq: the glow seen in the sky as the sun sets, i.e. the redness.
an Arab saying "a dyed garment as though it were the shafaq"
highlights.note: saying of the Arabs, recited by al-Farrāʾ

highlights.text: Mujāhid (one report via Ibn Najīḥ): "daytime" (al-nahār), on Q 84:16
treats sh-f-w through shafā, the edge of a thing
The shafā of a well or of anything else is its edge.
as in the Qur'an's ʿalā shafā jurufin, "on the brink of a bank" (Q 9:109)
a single semantic node meaning "to be on the brink of, to overlook, to come to the edge of"
healing is so called because it overcomes the illness and comes to stand over it.
al-ʿAjjāj: "I fulfilled it before a shafan, or at a shafan."
highlights.note: al-ʿAjjāj, Umayyad; the entry's only poet

highlights.text: al-shaghāf, "the covering of the heart"
he glosses as meaning that love reached, or penetrated as far as, the shaghāf
highlights.note: شَغَفَ, 1x; the entry's gloss of Q 12:30

highlights.text: "the opposite of being empty/free" (khilāf al-farāgh)
shaghaltu fulānan — "I occupied/busied so-and-so"
a verse is quoted where a woman greets someone and says that their group's departure "today" leaves them all mushtaghal
highlights.note: unattributed verse; the entry names no poet

highlights.text: one root meaning: whiteness set within something dark
Belonging to the same chapter is الشِّهَاب (shihāb): a blazing, shooting flame of fire.
a single root with one core meaning: presence, knowledge, and making-known
the word that pulls together all three strands: being present, knowing, and declaring
the place where people gather (a "presence" of people)
Al-Aʿshā uses both senses in a single line: "my shāhid" = his tongue, and "shāhid Allāh" = the angel.
because the angels of mercy attend (are present with) him
highlights.note: others' explanation of shahīd, one slain in God's path

highlights.text: Ibn Fāris reports the scholars' reading that shahida here means God "made known" / "made clear"
this root has one core meaning: height / elevation (ʿuluww).
الشَّهِيق (al-shahīq), meaning "inhalation" (drawing the breath back/up)
a single sound root meaning clarity/manifestness in a matter
named after the crescent and called a "month."
He cites Dhū al-Rumma as evidence — a verse describing someone keen-eyed who sees the crescent-month
highlights.note: Dhū al-Rumma, Umayyad; the entry's only poet
